desc:
Several piles of stones lie on the table. In a move, a player chooses one non-empty pile and removes at least one stone from it, so the pile becomes any size from 0 up to its current size minus 1. Players alternate. The player who cannot move, because every pile is empty, loses; equivalently, the player who takes the last stone wins.

Given the pile sizes piles, count the first moves that leave a position in which the second player, who moves next, is losing. A move is identified by its pile index and the new size of that pile, so each (pile, new size) pair is counted separately.

piles = [1, 2]    -> 1   (reduce the 2-pile to 1)
piles = [1, 2, 3] -> 0   (already a losing position for the player to move)
piles = [5]       -> 1   (take all 5 stones)
hints: Think about the position as a whole, not pile by pile. When is a position losing for the player who must move?
A position is losing exactly when the XOR (^) of all pile sizes is 0. A move changes one pile from x to a smaller size.
Let X be the XOR of all piles. To make the total XOR zero by changing pile x, its new size must be x ^ X, and that is a legal move only when x ^ X < x. Count the piles for which this holds.
editorial: This is Nim. The classic result (Bouton's theorem) says a position is losing for the player to move exactly when the XOR of the pile sizes is 0. From XOR 0 every move makes the XOR nonzero, and from a nonzero XOR some move always restores zero.

Let X be the total XOR. Changing a single pile x to make the total zero requires its new size to be exactly x ^ X, so each pile offers at most one winning move. That move is legal only when x ^ X < x. This holds precisely when the highest set bit of X is set in x: XOR with X clears that bit and leaves the higher bits of x unchanged, which makes the value smaller.
So the answer is the number of piles with (x ^ X) < x, found in one pass. When X is 0 no pile satisfies the test, so the formula gives 0 with no special case.
